prize_parts.citation: For the development of targeted protein degradation, in which small molecules such as PROTACs and molecular glues direct the ubiquitin-proteasome system to eliminate chosen proteins

statement.case_for: Targeted protein degradation is the one candidate that most of the committee ranks (all eight ballots include it, two of them first), and the support rests on content rather than habit. It introduces a genuinely new chemical modality: heterobifunctional molecules and molecular glues that reprogram an enzyme system to destroy a target instead of inhibiting it. The mechanism is chemically explicit (ligand design, ternary-complex formation, cereblon as the thalidomide target), it has been independently confirmed across many laboratories, and it has opened targets that occupancy-based inhibitors could not reach. As someone who works on how molecular machines exploit non-equilibrium processes, I find a small molecule that induces proximity and then turns catalytic turnover to its advantage an elegant concept. Having ranked it fourth in my opening, I now move it first because colleagues made clearer than my opening did that the credit can be divided cleanly into a concept strand (Crews and Deshaies) and a mechanism strand (Handa on cereblon), which yields a defensible three-person set.
statement.case_against: No degrader drug is yet approved, so therapeutic vindication of the modality is incomplete, and a prize now would be early compared with the sequencing and perovskite work I ranked higher. Attribution is also genuinely exclusionary: Ciulli (VHL ligands, structure-guided design), Ito (cereblon co-discoverer), Gray, Sakamoto and Kim all have substantive claims, and any three-person cut will be contested. The reservation I weigh most is that I am proposing this in part because it has the broadest support, and breadth of ranking is not by itself evidence of merit; if the first approvals slip or safety problems emerge, the choice will look premature. Sequencing by synthesis (B031) has two decades of proven impact, but its credit is commercially entangled and its status as chemistry is debated, which is why I no longer put it first.

responses.point: Aili ranks B063 first as a conceptually original new modality that makes small molecules programmable effectors of ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis, accepting that approvals are pending and the three-person cut is contestable.
responses.response: I agree on originality and on the mechanism, and your argument moved me up from fourth to first. I would qualify 'timely, arguably slightly early' more strongly than you do: the absence of an approved degrader is a real gap, not a footnote, because for a modality defined by its therapeutic promise the clinical proof is the final test. I accept your Crews-Deshaies-Handa trio as the least arbitrary attribution but would not call it clean.

responses.point: Somfai ranks Buchwald-Hartwig C-N coupling first as a general, step-economical method of undisputed industrial impact, and proposes a Crews-Ciulli-Handa trio for B063, excluding Deshaies.
responses.response: I take the C-N coupling case seriously and kept B032 among my top five, since its maturity is beyond question. My reservation is the 2010 cross-coupling prize, which makes it read as an extension of recognised chemistry rather than a new one, whereas degradation opens a new modality. On B063 I disagree with excluding Deshaies: the 2001 PROTAC paper was joint work, and dropping him would misstate priority. Ciulli's contribution is real but later and more optimising than founding, so I keep him out of the three.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranks proton-coupled electron transfer first as a unifying physical principle for respiration, photosynthesis and electrocatalysis, with decades of confirmation, and ranks B063 second while noting credit is split across PROTAC, cereblon and VHL chemistry.
responses.response: I agree that PCET is deep and mature, and as a physicist I appreciate the quantum treatment of the proton. My difficulty is that no other member ranked B025 and its attribution needs a three-way choice among four people with a theory/experiment split, whereas the field's influence is largely conceptual and harder to point to as one discovery. I would like to hear whether you can narrow it to a single sharply defined achievement. On B063 I share your worry about split credit and have handled it by crediting the concept and the cereblon mechanism, not the VHL chemistry.

responses.point: Sparr ranks ionizable lipid nanoparticles first as physical chemistry of lipid self-assembly turned into a delivery platform, valid at global scale and timely after the 2023 Medicine prize recognised the cargo but not the carrier.
responses.response: This is the strongest competing case and I do not dismiss it: the impact is beyond dispute and the chemical logic of pH-tuned lipids is clear. I am held back by attribution, since you, Aili, Åqvist and Chabes each propose a different trio from a crowded Vancouver, Cambridge and MIT field with patent entanglement. If the committee can agree on a defensible three, I would regard B035 as a serious rival to B063 and would not oppose it, but I do not yet see that agreement.

uncertainties: Whether the committee views the lack of an approved degrader as disqualifying now or only as a reason to prefer a later year.
Whether Deshaies, Ciulli or Ito should displace one of the three, and whether a prize split along PROTAC and glue lines is cleaner than a single part.
Whether ionizable lipid nanoparticles (B035) can be given a defensible three-person attribution, since I would otherwise weigh them equally with B063.
How much weight to give breadth of opening support versus the scientific merits of candidates ranked first by only one member.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile: none of the shortlisted candidates is tied to Lund University, NanoLund or my own research. I share Lund affiliation with Peter Somfai and Emma Sparr, which is an institutional connection among committee members and not to a candidate.
